title: AI Latency
shortDefinition: The time between sending a request to an AI model and receiving its response, critical for user-facing applications.
definition: AI latency is the time delay between sending a request to an AI model and receiving its response — a critical performance metric for any user-facing AI application, where slow response times directly degrade user experience. Latency is influenced by model size and complexity, input length, network conditions, and infrastructure configuration, and managing it well is essential for conversational AI, real-time recommendations, and any AI feature embedded in a live user interaction.

sections.title: What causes high AI latency
sections.description: Several factors drive AI response latency, from model size to infrastructure load.

content.text: Several factors drive AI response latency: model size (larger, more capable models generally take longer to generate a response), input and output length (more tokens to process and generate takes more time), network round-trip time to a remote API, and infrastructure load (high concurrent request volume without adequate scaling can introduce queueing delays). LLM responses also have a specific characteristic — generation happens token-by-token, meaning longer outputs inherently take proportionally longer, which is why streaming responses (showing text as it's generated, rather than waiting for the complete response) improves perceived latency even when total generation time is unchanged.

items: Model size — larger models generally take longer.
Input/output length — more tokens means more time.
Network round-trip — remote API calls add network delay.
Infrastructure load — queuing delays from high concurrency.
Token-by-token generation — longer outputs take proportionally longer.
Streaming — improves perceived latency even if total time is unchanged.

content.title: The key insight
content.text: Latency is influenced by factors across the entire stack — model, network, infrastructure, and application design.

Common latency reduction techniques include using smaller, faster models for tasks that don't require maximum capability, implementing caching for repeated or similar queries, streaming responses to improve perceived speed even before generation completes, reducing unnecessary context or prompt length, and choosing infrastructure with appropriate proximity and scaling to your user base. The right combination depends on your specific latency requirements and where in your application the delay is most noticeable to users.

items: Smaller models — faster for tasks that don't need maximum capability.
Caching — reduce repeated calls for similar queries.
Streaming — improve perceived speed before generation completes.
Prompt optimization — reduce unnecessary context or length.
Infrastructure proximity — choose regions closer to users.
Autoscaling — handle concurrent load without queueing delays.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of latency optimization

content.text: Latency optimization has limitations. There's often a tradeoff between latency and capability — smaller, faster models may produce lower quality outputs for complex tasks. Caching only helps for repeated queries, and streaming doesn't reduce total generation time. Network latency is outside your control for API-based models, and optimizing for latency can increase infrastructure cost or complexity. Some users may not notice moderate latency differences, and over-optimizing can waste resources.

items: Latency vs. capability tradeoff — smaller models may have lower quality.
Cache limitation — only helps for repeated queries.
Streaming — improves perception, not actual total time.
Network latency — outside your control for API-based models.
Cost tradeoff — optimization can increase infrastructure expense.
Diminishing returns — over-optimization may waste resources.

content.title: Important
content.text: Latency optimization is about meeting user expectations, not achieving the absolute minimum possible response time for its own sake.

sections.title: Best practices for AI latency optimization

content.text: Optimizing AI latency requires a systematic approach across model selection, infrastructure, and application design. The following practices can help ensure your AI application meets user expectations for speed.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Define latency targets based on user expectations for your specific context.
Measure current latency against real-world usage patterns.
Implement streaming for user-facing conversational applications.
Cache repeated or similar queries where appropriate.
Route simple tasks to smaller, faster models.
Optimize prompts to reduce unnecessary token usage.
Monitor latency in production and alert on degradation.
Balance latency optimization against output quality requirements.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure time-to-first-token (TTFT) for streaming responses and total response time for non-streaming. Both matter for different aspects of user experience.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about AI latency

items.question: What's an acceptable latency for a conversational AI application?
items.answer: This depends on user expectations for your specific context, but real-time conversational interfaces generally benefit from response times that feel immediate or near-immediate, often aided significantly by streaming.

items.question: Does streaming actually reduce latency, or just make it feel faster?
items.answer: Streaming improves perceived latency by showing output as it's generated rather than waiting for completion — total generation time may be similar, but the user experience feels significantly faster.

items.question: Can we reduce latency by using a smaller or cheaper model?
items.answer: Often yes, with some capability tradeoff — ClickMasters evaluates whether a smaller model maintains acceptable accuracy for your specific task before recommending this approach.

items.question: How do you measure latency in a way that reflects real user experience?
items.answer: ClickMasters measures against your specific real-world usage patterns and infrastructure conditions, not generic benchmark conditions that may not reflect actual deployment latency.

items.question: How long does a latency optimization project take?
items.answer: 6–16 weeks depending on whether it's an audit/optimization or a new multi-model routing architecture build.

items.question: Can latency optimization also reduce our AI API costs?
items.answer: Often yes — many of the same techniques (caching, appropriately-sized model routing) improve both latency and cost simultaneously.

items.question: What is time-to-first-token (TTFT)?
items.answer: TTFT is the time from sending a request to receiving the first token of the response. It's the key metric for perceived responsiveness in streaming implementations.

items.question: What is the difference between latency and throughput in AI systems?
items.answer: Latency is the time for a single request to be processed. Throughput is the number of requests a system can handle per second. Both matter — latency affects user experience, throughput affects scalability and cost.

items.question: Can edge computing help reduce AI latency?
items.answer: Yes — edge AI runs models on local devices, reducing or eliminating network round-trip time. This can dramatically reduce latency for applications that can run on edge hardware.

items.question: How do you handle latency spikes during high traffic periods?
items.answer: Latency spikes during high traffic can be managed through autoscaling infrastructure, request queuing, rate limiting, and caching. ClickMasters builds architecture that handles traffic variability gracefully.
